That’s just the beginning. You’ll feel it unravel. I’ll make sure of it.” Chapter 7 – Fractures The survivors gathered close to the fire, its glow a fragile shield against the endless dark. The Fog pressed close tonight — not enough to burn, but enough to feel. Like a wall just beyond the firelight, breathing with quiet intent. No one dared move too far from the circle. The scent of blood still clung to some of them, faint but sharp, as if the last trial hadn’t quite let go. Dwight’s words still clung in the air from the last report. A cuff. Sparks. Wesker faltering. Kate leaned forward, eyes glinting. “So what? We should be celebrating. His trials are easy now. We walk out breathing. That’s a win.” Her grin was sharp, but the tremor in her leg betrayed the leftover fear. Jake tossed a twig into the fire, leaning back with arms folded. “Finally, some balance. Guy was overpowered as hell. Maybe the Fog finally nerfed him.” “He still threw me over a generator,” Meg muttered. “And I’m not gonna pretend he didn’t enjoy it.” “Well, maybe now he limps while he does it,” Jake quipped, but the way his fingers picked at a fading bruise on his jaw betrayed the memory of a very recent hit. Claudette wrung her hands, gaze fixed on the flames. “You didn’t see him. He wasn’t just slower. He looked... sick. Like it’s killing him.” Meg scoffed, but her voice wavered. “He’s still the one throwing us on hooks. Don’t forget that. If he’s hurting, good. He deserves worse.” Nea’s voice slipped in, hesitant but firm. “Still doesn’t feel right. Whatever else he is... he’s stuck here just like us. All the killers are. If he’s breaking down, that’s not a win. That’s—” “—that’s one less monster breathing down our necks,” Jake cut in, sharp. “I’m not losing sleep over it.” The fire popped. Silence weighed heavy. Some sat straighter, pride in their eyes at the thought of easier trials. Others hunched lower, unsettled by the image of a killer reduced to almost nothing overnight. A line had clearly been drawn — pragmatists on one side, bleeding hearts on the other. Dwight sat quiet, shoulders tense. He had seen it up close. Wesker’s snarl, his hand at his throat, and the look in his eyes as that power was stripped away in an instant. He could still feel the glow of the cuff radiating heat against his skin, and the way Wesker’s hand had spasmed away from him. He didn’t speak again. He didn’t have to. The fracture was already spreading rampant through the camp. Arguments grew sharper with each return to the fire. Meg’s bravado turned scathing. Jake mocked anyone who dared suggest sympathy. Feng puffed herself up, boasting about how easy her escapes had become. Claudette pleaded for caution, voice thin but insistent. “You don’t understand — if something can control him, then what stops it from controlling the others? What if we’re next?” Her pleas only earned her contempt back. “You sound crazy,” Meg snapped. “It’s not our problem. Let it break him.” The camp fractured further. Survivors started refusing to share strategies. Old habits died first — item swaps, generator routes, killer callouts. In one trial, Elodie lay slumped by a hook near the Asylum gates, bleeding out and begging quietly for help. Feng vaulted past without so much as a glance. “Should’ve picked a side,” she muttered. In another, Nea staggered toward Meg with a medkit outstretched, only to be waved off and left behind. The compassionate ones were ostracized, left whispering to each other in smaller clusters, tension thick as the firelight flickered across their faces. No one looked each other in the eye anymore. Through it all, Gabriel sat silent, his dark eyes thoughtful as the arguments flew. Dwight’s earlier insistence about the black band had set off something in his mind that he couldn’t quite let go. When some of the more antagonistic survivors had been taken by the Fog for trials, Gabriel took the opportunity to join Dwight at the fire. “Describe it to me. The cuff.” Dwight blinked at him. “What?” “You said it was seamless. Sparking. Fused to his skin. Tell me everything you saw.” Dwight swallowed, then recounted the details — the red glow, the sparks, the way Wesker clutched at it as if trying to tear it off. Claudette added her own memory of his faltering swings. Nea mentioned the way he staggered between hits. Gabriel’s frown deepened with every word. “It sounds almost like some kind of conductor. I doubt it’s actually seamless, it had to be applied to him somehow, but it sounds like it’s been screwing up his attacks for a while now,” he nodded, thoughtfully. His voice was calm, but the words carried weight. “If it’s actively controlling him, and that’s a huge IF, then it’s a risk to all of us. Rules are the only thing that let us survive in here. If something can break those rules, it’s not just his problem. It’s ours.” Uneasy silence followed. Even some of the pragmatists looked shaken, murmuring amongst each other with significantly less confidence than they had earlier. Gabriel rose slowly, dusting ash from his hands. “That settles it then. I need to see it myself. Up close.” He wasn’t foolish — getting close to a killer was a death sentence more often than not. But the real threat wasn’t Wesker’s claws. It was the silence from the Entity. The rules didn’t bend. They weren’t supposed to bend. “Are you sure about this?” Claudette followed him across the camp, clearly concerned.
